title: Hollywood 1930–1990 (comparative study): Casablanca vs Bonnie and Clyde

items.definition: A cynical American exile learns to give up private love for the fight against fascism: a wartime call to commitment.
items.examples: Rick moves from “I stick my neck out for nobody” to “the problems of three little people don’t amount to a hill of beans in this crazy world.”
keyFacts: Rick’s arc mirrors America’s: from neutral isolationism to joining the war, so a personal story carries a national message
Set in December 1941, the days around Pearl Harbor (“If it’s December 1941 in Casablanca, what time is it in New York?”)
The peak of the Classical Hollywood style: invisible editing, star system, goal-driven hero and full closure
Killer line: “Curtiz’s studio-era classic turns Rick’s private sacrifice into propaganda for American intervention, proving the Classical style could carry an urgent political context.”
items.examTip: Use Rick’s arc as your spine for any context question: his personal choice stands for America’s choice in 1941–42.

items.term: Historical context: the Second World War
items.definition: Made in 1942 and set in December 1941, as the USA entered the war after Pearl Harbor (7 December 1941).
items.examples: The film premiered in New York in November 1942, weeks after Allied forces landed in North Africa and took Casablanca.
keyFacts: Vichy France collaborated with Nazi Germany, so French Morocco is a grey zone where Nazis, Vichy police and refugees mix
Renault drops a bottle of Vichy water in the bin at the end: France symbolically rejects collaboration
The topical timing made the title front-page news, a lucky break the studio exploited for publicity
items.examTip: Link a specific moment (the Vichy water, the Marseillaise) to the war, not just “it was made in WW2”.

items.definition: Many Americans opposed joining the war until Pearl Harbor; Rick’s neutrality and conversion mirror that national shift.
items.examples: Rick refuses to help Ugarte (“I stick my neck out for nobody”) but finally shoots Strasser and sends Laszlo to carry on the resistance.
keyFacts: The government’s Office of War Information encouraged Hollywood films that supported the war effort
Laszlo (resistance leader) is the ideal of commitment; Rick becomes the reluctant hero America needed
The final “beautiful friendship” of an American and a Frenchman suggests the Allied alliance
items.examTip: A political reading is strongest when you show HOW form delivers it, e.g. the anthem duel’s cutting.

items.definition: Casablanca is a waiting room for refugees fleeing Nazi Europe, desperate for exit visas to Lisbon and America.
items.examples: The opening map traces the refugee trail Paris → Marseilles → Oran → Casablanca → Lisbon → America.
keyFacts: Nearly all the cast were immigrants, many of them refugees from Nazi Europe: a film about refugees made by refugees
The Bulgarian bride subplot (Annina) shows refugees forced into corruption; Rick rigs the roulette to save her
America is presented as the promised land, a flattering self-image for 1942 audiences
items.examTip: Social context + representation: refugees, gender roles and nationality all come from the same wartime moment.

items.term: Institutional context: Warner Bros. studio system
items.definition: A vertically integrated studio film made by contract staff: producer Hal B. Wallis, director Michael Curtiz.
items.examples: Warner Bros. bought the unproduced play “Everybody Comes to Rick’s” (Murray Burnett and Joan Alison) for $20,000; Julius and Philip Epstein and Howard Koch wrote the screenplay.
keyFacts: Contract stars (Humphrey Bogart), composer (Max Steiner), cinematographer (Arthur Edeson) and editor (Owen Marks) were studio employees assigned to the film
Shot at Warner’s Burbank studios, not on location, from 25 May to 3 August 1942: 59 days, 11 over schedule
The script was still unfinished when cameras rolled; the writers were also shaping it to satisfy the Production Code
The release was moved forward to exploit the headlines after the Allies landed at Casablanca in November 1942
items.examTip: Production-context questions: contrast this factory model with Beatty’s independent producing on Bonnie and Clyde.

items.definition: Hollywood’s self-censorship rules (from 1934): no sympathetic adultery, crime must be punished, sex kept off screen.
items.examples: The airport ending: as a married woman, Ilsa must leave with Laszlo, so the Code helps decide the resolution.
keyFacts: Ilsa is married to Laszlo, so the Code made it almost impossible for her to leave with Rick
The censors objected to Renault trading visas for sex; the dialogue keeps it implied
Ellipsis and dissolves were the Classical way of suggesting what could not be shown
items.examTip: A strong context point: the Code shaped the narrative resolution, not just what was cut.

items.definition: A 1943 hit that won Best Picture, Director and Screenplay Oscars, then grew into one of the most loved films ever.
items.examples: Umberto Eco: “Two clichés make us laugh. A hundred clichés move us.”
keyFacts: Eco argued Casablanca is a “collage” of genre clichés (war film, romance, thriller) that adds up to a myth
Repeated TV and repertory screenings created its cult following, especially among students in the 1950s–60s
Its lines (“Here’s looking at you, kid”, “Round up the usual suspects”) entered everyday speech
items.examTip: Reception history lets you argue the film’s meaning changed over time, a sophisticated context point.

items.definition: Arthur Edeson’s chiaroscuro lighting fills the café and offices with shadows, bars and blinds: a world of entrapment.
items.examples: Shadows of window blinds fall across Rick and Renault; the airport is lit through fog with hard backlight.
keyFacts: Edeson had shot The Maltese Falcon (1941) with Bogart, and Casablanca shares its proto-noir look
Bars of shadow suggest everyone in Casablanca is a prisoner waiting for a visa
Three-point lighting is used classically to model faces and pick the star out of the crowd
items.examTip: Name the lighting AND its meaning: “barred shadows connote entrapment”.

items.definition: Ilsa is lit with soft, diffused light and eye catchlights so her face glows: the idealised object of Rick’s gaze.
items.examples: Her first close-up as she asks Sam to “play it” is softer and brighter than the shots around it.
keyFacts: Classical Hollywood glamour lighting turned stars into icons; Bergman’s close-ups are held longer than other characters’
The soft light connotes purity and romance even though her story involves a secret past
Mulvey’s idea of woman as “to-be-looked-at” is useful here: the camera adopts Rick’s gaze
items.examTip: Good for gender/representation and for the star as a contributor to meaning.

items.definition: The café is a microcosm of wartime Europe: every nation, class and loyalty under one roof, run by an American.
items.examples: Props that matter: the letters of transit, the rigged roulette wheel, the chess set Rick plays alone, the piano where Sam plays.
keyFacts: Rick’s white tuxedo marks him as separate and in control; Strasser’s uniform marks Nazi menace
The café has a public front (gambling, music) and a private back office: Rick’s divided self
The Moorish arches and lamps are studio exotic, a Hollywood fantasy of North Africa
items.examTip: Pick two props and track how their meaning changes (the letters of transit drive the whole plot).

items.definition: Invisible continuity editing (shot/reverse shot, eyeline matches, 180° rule) keeps the spectator absorbed in the story.
items.examples: The Rick–Ilsa conversations are built from matched close-ups; the Paris flashback is entered and left by dissolves.
keyFacts: Editor Owen Marks was Oscar-nominated for Best Film Editing; the style hides the cut so meaning seems to come from the characters
The opening montage (map, globe, newsreel-style voiceover) borrows documentary techniques to set the context
Contrast with Dede Allen’s jump cuts in Bonnie and Clyde, which make the editing visible
items.examTip: Classical editing is a comparison goldmine: invisible vs visible editing = studio era vs New Hollywood.

items.term: Sound: Max Steiner’s score and “As Time Goes By”
items.definition: Steiner’s score uses leitmotifs: the song “As Time Goes By” becomes the theme of Rick and Ilsa’s lost love.
items.examples: Sam plays the song diegetically; Steiner then weaves it into the non-diegetic score at every romantic memory.
keyFacts: “La Marseillaise” is used as a leitmotif of France and resistance, and swells over the final walk into the fog
Fragments of the German anthem are distorted in the score to signal Nazi threat
The diegetic/non-diegetic shift lets music move from the café into the characters’ memories
items.examTip: Use “leitmotif” and “diegetic to non-diegetic” for top-band terminology.

items.definition: Bogart brings his tough, cynical gangster/detective persona, then lets it crack to show the wounded romantic beneath.
items.examples: Drunk and alone in the dark café: “Of all the gin joints in all the towns in all the world, she walks into mine.”
keyFacts: Minimal, restrained gesture and clipped delivery: emotion is shown in pauses and the tightening of his face
Claude Rains’s witty Renault and Paul Henreid’s stiff, noble Laszlo frame Rick between cynicism and idealism
Richard Dyer’s star theory: a star image is a set of meanings the audience brings to every role
items.examTip: Star = a possible “auteur” for the auteur question: the film is as much Bogart’s as Curtiz’s.

items.term: Opening: the globe and the refugee trail
items.definition: A spinning globe, an animated map and a newsreel-style voiceover set the wartime context before the story starts.
items.examples: The camera then cranes down into the market as police round up suspects; a man carrying Free French papers is shot.
keyFacts: Documentary techniques (voiceover, map) give the fiction authority and topicality
The Cross of Lorraine on the dead man’s leaflets signals the Free French resistance
The crane movement from the sky into the street is a Curtiz signature of fluid camera
items.examTip: Perfect evidence for “reflects historical/political context”: the film tells you its context in the first minute.

items.definition: Nazi officers sing “Die Wacht am Rhein”; Laszlo has the band play “La Marseillaise” and the whole café drowns them out.
items.examples: Rick nods to the bandleader: his first public act of commitment. Yvonne, who flirted with a German, sings in tears: “Vive la France!”
keyFacts: Fast cutting between singing faces turns the café into a nation united against Nazism
Sound is the battlefield: two diegetic songs compete and the louder one wins
Renault closes the café: “I’m shocked, shocked to find that gambling is going on in here!”
items.examTip: The single best scene for political context + sound + editing in Casablanca.

items.definition: In fog, Rick sends Ilsa away with Laszlo, shoots Strasser, and walks off with Renault: love sacrificed for the cause.
items.examples: “We’ll always have Paris.” “Here’s looking at you, kid.” Renault: “Round up the usual suspects.” “Louis, I think this is the beginning of a beautiful friendship.”
keyFacts: Low-key lighting through studio fog makes the set feel mythic and hides its small scale
Full classical closure: every narrative strand is resolved and the hero is reintegrated into society
“La Marseillaise” swells as they walk into the fog: personal story becomes national myth
items.examTip: Compare with Bonnie and Clyde’s ending: closure and hope vs abrupt death and a cut to black.

items.definition: Rick is tough, self-reliant and wounded; true manhood is shown as self-sacrifice for a greater cause.
items.examples: Laszlo is the noble ideal; Rick is the flawed man who earns heroism by giving up Ilsa.
keyFacts: Wartime ideology: men must put duty before desire
Rick makes every key decision, including Ilsa’s future
Renault’s sexual exploitation of refugees is played as charm, a period blind spot
items.examTip: Gender questions: connect masculinity to the war-effort ideology.

items.term: Femininity: Ilsa as object of exchange
items.definition: Ilsa is passed between two men; her desire matters less than the men’s decisions and the war.
items.examples: “You’ll have to think for both of us.” Rick decides she will leave with Laszlo.
keyFacts: Glamour lighting makes her an image to be looked at (Mulvey)
Yvonne, the discarded lover, is punished for flirting with a German
Annina must consider sleeping with Renault to get visas: women’s bodies as currency
items.examTip: Contrast with Bonnie, who drives the action and voices her own desire.

items.definition: Americans are the moral centre, Nazis are cold villains, the French are redeemed; Sam is talented but subordinate.
items.examples: Sam (Dooley Wilson) is called “boy” by Ilsa and exists mainly to serve Rick’s story.
keyFacts: Strasser is a propaganda caricature of Nazi arrogance
Renault’s conversion stands for France turning from Vichy to resistance
Sam is loyal and gifted, but Classical Hollywood gives Black characters little inner life
items.examTip: A modern oppositional reading of Sam’s role shows a critical, sophisticated approach.

items.definition: Hungarian émigré and Warner contract director: fast, versatile, with a fluid camera and expressive shadows.
items.examples: Also directed The Adventures of Robin Hood (1938), Yankee Doodle Dandy (1942) and Mildred Pierce (1945).
keyFacts: Signatures: crane and tracking shots through crowded sets, foreground objects in the frame, strong shadows
He made films in almost every genre, which makes a single thematic signature hard to find
Sarris put him in his “Lightly Likable” category, far below the Pantheon of true auteurs
Sarris saw him as reflecting “the strengths and weaknesses of the studio system”: a craftsman more than an author
items.examTip: Argue “how far”: a strong STYLISTIC signature, a weak THEMATIC one.

items.term: Casablanca as collaborative “genius of the system”
items.definition: Thomas Schatz argued studio films were authored by the system: producers, writers, stars and craft departments together.
items.examples: Wallis chose the project and team; the Epsteins wrote the wit; Koch the politics; Steiner the music; Edeson the look; Bogart the persona.
keyFacts: Schatz, The Genius of the System (1988): producers like Wallis were often as decisive as directors
The film’s success is often called a “happy accident” of studio teamwork
This makes Casablanca the perfect film to TEST auteur theory rather than simply apply it
items.examTip: Band 5 indicative content rewards recognising institutional limits on the auteur.

items.definition: A star’s persona can shape meaning as strongly as a director’s style: Bogart’s cynical hero defines the film.
items.examples: Bogart’s earlier roles in High Sierra and The Maltese Falcon (both 1941) built the image the audience brought to Rick.
keyFacts: The mark scheme accepts any significant role as auteur: director, cinematographer, star, editor, composer or studio
Dyer: stars are constructed images with meanings that carry between films
Compare Warren Beatty, star AND producer of Bonnie and Clyde
items.examTip: Arguing for a non-director auteur shows independent thinking.

items.term: Bonnie and Clyde: the key idea
items.definition: 1930s outlaws remade as glamorous, rebellious anti-heroes: a Depression story speaking to 1960s youth and violence.
items.examples: “We rob banks.” The gang are cheered by poor farmers, then destroyed by the state in a shocking ambush.
keyFacts: Comic, romantic and suddenly brutal: the tonal shifts were new for a Hollywood film
The audience is aligned with the criminals against the law, an anti-establishment stance
Often named as the film that launched New Hollywood
Killer line: “Penn uses European art-cinema techniques to turn Depression outlaws into 1960s counterculture martyrs, making the spectator feel the real cost of violence.”
items.examTip: Every context point has two layers: the 1930s setting and the 1960s production.

items.definition: Set in 1930s Texas and the Midwest, when bank foreclosures, poverty and the Dust Bowl made robbers into folk heroes.
items.examples: The real Barrow gang robbed and killed across the South-West until Bonnie Parker and Clyde Barrow were ambushed in Louisiana in May 1934.
keyFacts: Banks repossessing farms made them hated, so robbing them looked like revenge for the poor
Bonnie’s real poem “The Story of Bonnie and Clyde” is read in the film: they built their own legend
The film romanticises and simplifies the real gang, who killed several police officers
items.examTip: Don’t confuse setting with production context: the 1930s is the story, the 1960s is the context that shaped it.

items.definition: Vietnam on TV, civil rights struggles, assassinations and a youth counterculture distrusting authority shaped the film.
items.examples: Penn said TV images of the Vietnam War, broadcast daily while he was filming, shaped the climax; the piece of Clyde’s scalp shot away was meant to evoke the Zapruder film of Kennedy’s assassination.
keyFacts: Penn later said he considered the film to be “about Vietnam”: a film of the 1960s, not the 1930s
He said TV coverage of Vietnam was as bloody as anything in his film
Young audiences identified with outsiders rebelling against a corrupt establishment
items.examTip: Social context + spectatorship: young audiences cheered the outlaws; older critics were appalled.

items.term: Institutional context: the end of the studio system
items.definition: After the 1948 Paramount ruling and TV, studios lost power; independent producers and young directors gained it.
items.examples: Warner Bros.–Seven Arts had so little faith in the film that it gave first-time producer Warren Beatty 40% of the gross instead of a fee.
keyFacts: Jack Warner reportedly treated the project as a whim of Beatty’s
After a weak first run, Beatty pushed Warner into a wider release; the 1968 re-release made it one of the year’s biggest hits
Shot largely on real Texas locations, not studio backlots: cheaper and more realistic
items.examTip: Compare with Casablanca’s factory model for any production-context question.

items.term: Censorship: the collapse of the Production Code
items.definition: By 1967 the Code was failing; graphic violence and frank sexuality helped push its 1968 replacement by age ratings.
items.examples: Bloody squibs, a man shot in the face through glass, and Clyde’s impotence would all have been unthinkable in 1942.
keyFacts: The MPAA ratings system (G, M, R, X) replaced the Code in November 1968
Sex is discussed openly but Clyde cannot perform, a bold twist on the gangster hero
Compare Casablanca’s dissolve to the searchlight: implication vs exposure
items.examTip: One of the clearest comparison points between the two films.

items.term: Cultural context: the French New Wave
items.definition: Writers David Newman and Robert Benton loved the French New Wave and first offered the script to Truffaut and Godard.
items.examples: Jump cuts, sudden shifts from comedy to violence, and a doomed romantic couple on the run all echo Godard’s Breathless (1960).
keyFacts: The spec: New Hollywood directors “began to show new influences, especially from European cinema”
Location shooting, handheld moments and elliptical editing break classical rules
Robert Towne did uncredited rewrites on set
items.examTip: Cultural context = an artistic movement; name it precisely: “the French New Wave (Nouvelle Vague)”.

items.definition: The film split critics: Bosley Crowther attacked it, Pauline Kael defended it, and the younger view won.
items.examples: Bosley Crowther of the New York Times called it “a cheap piece of bald-faced slapstick comedy”; Pauline Kael wrote a 9,000-word defence published in The New Yorker in October 1967.
keyFacts: Ten Oscar nominations; it won two: Estelle Parsons (Supporting Actress) and Burnett Guffey (Cinematography)
McCall’s refused to run Kael’s review; The New Yorker printed it in full, and it became a landmark of film criticism
Some historians argue Kael’s review did not “save” the film alone: Beatty’s push for a re-release mattered too
items.examTip: Reception splits by generation: perfect for a spectatorship angle in a context answer.

items.definition: Real locations and soft natural light give a sun-faded, nostalgic 1930s look, broken by brutal close-ups.
items.examples: Bonnie’s lips in extreme close-up in the opening; the ending uses several cameras at different speeds for slow motion.
keyFacts: Guffey won the Oscar for Best Cinematography
Soft light romanticises the couple; harsh close-ups of wounds shatter the romance
Wide shots of empty landscapes make the gang look small and exposed
items.examTip: Contrast with Edeson’s studio chiaroscuro in Casablanca.

items.definition: Dede Allen’s fast, elliptical cutting and jump cuts make the editing visible and the tone unstable.
items.examples: The ending mixes split-second cuts between Bonnie and Clyde’s faces with slow-motion shots of their bodies hit by bullets.
keyFacts: Influenced by the French New Wave and by Eisenstein’s montage (the shot through the glass)
Abrupt cuts from comedy to violence stop the spectator settling into one response
Allen became one of the most influential editors of New Hollywood
items.examTip: Use “elliptical editing”, “jump cut” and “montage” for terminology marks.

items.definition: Flatt and Scruggs’ jaunty bluegrass banjo plays over the getaways, making crime feel like a comic adventure.
items.examples: The banjo plays as the gang escape from robberies, even as the chases turn dangerous.
keyFacts: Often contrapuntal: cheerful music against real danger creates unease
The music disappears as the film darkens; the ending has no score, just birds, gunfire and silence
Period-appropriate folk music adds Depression-era authenticity
items.examTip: Compare with Steiner’s emotional leitmotif score in Casablanca.

items.definition: Theadora Van Runkle’s stylish costumes, the getaway cars and the guns turn the outlaws into glamorous icons.
items.examples: Bonnie’s beret and midi skirts; Clyde showing Bonnie his gun at the start, which she strokes.
keyFacts: The gun works as a phallic symbol that compensates for Clyde’s impotence (a Freudian reading)
Cars = freedom and escape, but also the trap where they die
Dusty small towns and foreclosed farmhouses ground the glamour in poverty
items.examTip: Track a motif (the gun, the car) from opening to ending.

items.definition: Naturalistic, often improvised, Method-influenced acting gives the gang a raw, modern feel unlike 1940s star polish.
items.examples: Faye Dunaway’s restless frustration; Warren Beatty’s charm and insecurity; Estelle Parsons’ screaming Blanche.
keyFacts: Gene Hackman (Buck) and Michael J. Pollard (C.W. Moss) added comic, earthy energy
Performances make the outlaws likeable, so their deaths hurt
Compare Bogart’s controlled star performance
items.examTip: Performance comparison: classical star persona vs New Hollywood naturalism.

items.definition: Sepia snapshots with camera clicks, then an extreme close-up of Bonnie’s red lips as she prowls naked and bored.
items.examples: She leans on her bed frame, its rails like prison bars, then sees Clyde trying to steal her mother’s car.
keyFacts: Opens on female desire, unheard of in a 1940s film
The bars connote small-town entrapment; Clyde is her escape
The photo-album credits frame the story as a legend being recorded
items.examTip: Perfect opening comparison with Casablanca’s documentary-style globe.

items.definition: During a robbery a bank employee jumps on the getaway car; Clyde shoots him in the face through the glass.
items.examples: A shocking close-up of the bloodied face; afterwards the gang hide in a cinema watching “We’re in the Money” from Gold Diggers of 1933.
keyFacts: The tone flips from slapstick to horror in one cut: Dede Allen’s editing makes the shock land
The close-up recalls Eisenstein’s Odessa Steps shot of a woman shot through her glasses
The Hollywood musical they watch is the escapism of the old cinema, contrasted with new realism
items.examTip: Strong for New Hollywood vs Classical: the film literally shows a 1930s musical inside itself.

items.definition: Birds scatter, the lovers exchange a look, and a hail of bullets plays in slow motion; then a sudden cut to black.
items.examples: Rapid cuts between their faces, then multi-speed slow motion as their bodies jerk under gunfire; no music, no resolution.
keyFacts: Called a “ballet of death”: aestheticised yet horrifying violence
No restored equilibrium, no moral voiceover: the spectator is left in shock
The establishment kills its rebels: a powerful image for 1967 audiences
items.examTip: Compare directly with Casablanca’s closure: fog, music and friendship vs silence and death.

items.term: Gender: Bonnie’s desire and Clyde’s impotence
items.definition: Bonnie is active and desiring; Clyde’s impotence undermines the macho gangster hero.
items.examples: Clyde: “I ain’t much of a lover boy.” Late in the film they finally make love after Bonnie’s poem is published.
keyFacts: Reflects 1960s debates about sexuality and women’s liberation
Blanche is a comic stereotype of hysterical femininity
Clyde’s confidence comes from guns and fame, not traditional masculinity
items.examTip: Compare with Ilsa’s passivity and Rick’s mastery in Casablanca.

items.definition: The outlaws are likeable folk heroes; the law (Frank Hamer) is cold, humourless and finally vengeful.
items.examples: The gang photograph themselves with a captured Hamer, humiliating him; he returns to kill them.
keyFacts: Anti-establishment ideology aligned with the 1960s counterculture
Spectators are positioned to sympathise with criminals: a break from the Code’s rule that crime must not pay
C.W.’s father betrays them to the police for a deal
items.examTip: Useful ideological link even though Section A foregrounds context and auteur.

items.term: Violence: the end of the clean death
items.definition: Violence is graphic and messy, with squibs and blood, so killing has visible physical cost.
items.examples: The bank clerk’s face; Buck’s head wound; the final slow-motion bullets.
keyFacts: In Classical Hollywood people died cleanly; here bodies are damaged
Penn argued realistic violence was more moral than bloodless violence
Opened the way for the violence of later New Hollywood (The Wild Bunch, 1969)
items.examTip: Compare Strasser’s quick, bloodless death in Casablanca.

items.definition: Penn came from live TV and theatre; his films return to outsiders, violence and myths of American history.
items.examples: The Left Handed Gun (1958, Billy the Kid), The Miracle Worker (1962), Little Big Man (1970).
keyFacts: Thematic signature: sympathetic rebels destroyed by a violent society
Stylistic signature: actor-centred, naturalistic performance and bursts of physical violence
Penn insisted on shooting in Texas for authenticity
items.examTip: Show both stylistic AND thematic signatures for top bands.

items.term: Bonnie and Clyde as collaborative authorship
items.definition: Beatty (star-producer), Benton and Newman (writers), Allen (editor) and Guffey (camera) all shaped the film.
items.examples: Beatty fought the studio for the film; Allen’s editing is often credited with its rhythm and shock.
keyFacts: The 2019 examiners’ report praised candidates who recognised specific crew members’ contributions to Bonnie and Clyde
Beatty is arguably the film’s driving force, so the “auteur” could be the producer-star
New Hollywood promoted the director-auteur image even though work stayed collaborative
items.examTip: Examiners reward naming specific collaborators: do it in every auteur answer.

items.term: New Hollywood and the auteur renaissance
items.definition: From the late 1960s young directors gained unusual control over their films in a weakened studio system.
items.examples: Bonnie and Clyde and The Graduate (both 1967) are usually named as the start; Peter Biskind’s Easy Riders, Raging Bulls tells the story.
keyFacts: Directors were influenced by European art cinema and by auteur criticism itself
Sarris brought auteur theory to America in 1962, so directors began to see themselves as authors
Ended around 1980 as blockbusters returned power to studios
items.examTip: Context + auteur together: the institution changed, so authorship changed.

topics.title: Comparing the films and the auteur approach

items.term: Classical style vs New Hollywood style
items.definition: Casablanca hides its technique to absorb the viewer; Bonnie and Clyde shows it to jolt the viewer.
items.examples: Continuity editing and studio sets vs jump cuts, location shooting and tonal shifts.

comparisonTable.title: Style compared
rows: Location, soft natural light, slow motion
Bluegrass counterpoint, silence at the end

keyFacts: Classical: goal-driven hero, cause and effect, closure (Bordwell)
New Hollywood: ambiguity, anti-heroes, open or bleak endings
Both are still genre films (war-romance, gangster) that bend their genres
items.examTip: Compare WITHIN each paragraph using “whereas” and “similarly”.

items.definition: A studio-assigned project made in a factory system vs a star-produced project made as the studio system collapsed.
items.examples: Wallis assigned Curtiz, Bogart and Steiner; Beatty chose Penn, hired the team and owned a share of the profits.
keyFacts: Studio era: contracts, sound stages, the Production Code
Post-studio era: independent producers, locations, the move to ratings
The sample paper asks: “Compare how far your chosen films reflect their different production contexts.”
items.examTip: This is a real exam question: have a 4-paragraph plan ready.

items.definition: Rick sacrifices love and rejoins society; Bonnie and Clyde refuse society and are destroyed by it.
items.examples: Rick walks into the fog with Renault; Bonnie and Clyde die in a hail of bullets.
keyFacts: 1942: individual desire must serve the collective war effort
1967: the individual rebels against a corrupt establishment
Both protagonists are outsiders who make a final defining choice
items.examTip: Use endings as your conclusion evidence: they crystallise each era’s values.

items.definition: Casablanca is set just a year before its release; Bonnie and Clyde looks back 30 years to talk about its own present.
items.examples: Casablanca’s refugees were real in 1942; Bonnie and Clyde’s Depression rebels stand for 1960s youth.
keyFacts: A period film reflects the time it was MADE as much as the time it SHOWS
Both films romanticise their subjects
Context questions reward recognising this double layer
items.examTip: A subtle comparison point that lifts answers into the top band.

items.term: La politique des auteurs (Cahiers du Cinéma)
items.definition: 1950s French critics, led by Truffaut, argued the director is the true author whose personal vision marks every film.
items.examples: Truffaut’s essay “A Certain Tendency of French Cinema” (1954); Cahiers praised Hollywood directors such as Hitchcock and Hawks.
keyFacts: Claimed even studio directors could express a personal vision through style (mise-en-scène)
Distinguished auteurs from mere “metteurs en scène” (technicians)
The same critics then became New Wave directors, influencing Bonnie and Clyde
items.examTip: Link the theory to the films: the New Wave connects auteur theory to Bonnie and Clyde directly.

items.definition: Sarris (1962) said an auteur shows technical competence, a distinguishable personal style and an “interior meaning”.
items.examples: His book The American Cinema (1968) ranked directors, with a “Pantheon” at the top.
keyFacts: Brought auteur theory into American criticism
Interior meaning = the tension between a director’s personality and the material
Useful test: does Curtiz have interior meaning, or only competence and style?
items.examTip: Apply the three circles to each director in turn for a structured auteur answer.

items.term: Pauline Kael and the case against auteurism
items.definition: Kael’s “Circles and Squares” (1963) attacked Sarris: films are collaborative and repeated habits are not genius.
items.examples: Ironically Kael championed Bonnie and Clyde, a film shaped by many creative voices.
keyFacts: Argues writers, stars and editors deserve credit
Points out that a recognisable signature can just be repetition
Supports a collaborative reading of both films
items.examTip: Use Kael to evaluate (AO2): auteur theory has limits.

items.definition: Auteur theory explains signature style but can ignore collaboration, institutions, stars and audiences.
items.examples: Barthes’ “The Death of the Author” (1967) moves meaning to the reader; Schatz moves it to the studio.
keyFacts: Strength: explains recurring style and themes across a director’s work
Weakness: Casablanca shows how much a studio and its crafts shaped a film
Middle ground: the director as orchestrator of a team’s talents
items.examTip: The question says “how far”: always reach a judgement on the approach itself.
